title: Working with velvet yarn
subtitle: Reading stitches and maintaining tension in plush cut-pile yarn
excerpt: Velvet yarn is a cut-pile yarn that produces a dense plush surface. The pile makes it difficult to see individual stitches once they are worked, which is the main challenge. The technique is standard crochet, but you need to feel the stitch insertion point rather than see it.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A yarn with a cut pile construction, produced by weaving short fibres around a core strand and then cutting them to create a dense, soft surface. The pile obscures the stitch structure.
The two loops that form the V-shape at the top of a completed stitch, into which the hook is normally inserted for the following row.

content.text: is a cut-pile yarn: a dense plush pile wraps a central core strand, producing a fabric with a soft, deep surface. The technique for crocheting with it is the same as for any other yarn, but the pile hides the stitch structure completely. You cannot see the
once a row is worked. This makes counting and inserting the hook for the next row more difficult than usual.

items.name: Velvet or chenille yarn
items.note: Usually aran or chunky weight. Nylon-based velvet yarns are the most common; polyester versions are similar to handle.

items.name: Crochet hook, 5.0 mm to 6.5 mm
items.note: The hook size on the label; velvet yarn is unforgiving if you go too far down in hook size.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.note: Essential. Place one at each end of every row to count stitches reliably.

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.note: For sewing in tails. Velvet does not frog well; tails need to be firmly secured.

items.name: Good light
items.note: A bright lamp angled across the fabric helps pick out the stitch line under the pile.

content.text: The key technique is feeling for the stitch rather than looking for it. Hold the fabric with your non-dominant hand and pinch the row below lightly between thumb and forefinger. The stitch tops are the slight ridges you feel under your thumb at regular intervals. Insert the hook at each ridge point, pushing through the pile until you feel the hook pass through the stitch loop below the surface.
Before starting: place a stitch marker in the first and last stitch of the foundation row. These anchors let you count from the ends rather than searching the middle for lost stitches.

At the start of each row: count the number of stitches from one marker to the other by running your finger along the top of the previous row, feeling for the stitch ridges. Count before you work; do not rely on counting as you go.
Insert the hook through both loops of the stitch top with a slight downward push. In velvet yarn, the hook often needs to be pushed 3 to 5 mm deeper than usual to clear the pile.
Work each stitch at a consistent tension. Velvet yarn tends to obscure loose stitches until they become apparent in the blocking stage.
Move stitch markers up at the end of every two or three rows. Do not leave them in the same stitch for too long or the pile will be distorted when you remove them.

Velvet yarn does not undo well. The pile mats and distorts when the stitches are pulled out, and the result looks worn in the unworked sections. Tink (undo stitch by stitch) rather than frogging if you need to correct an error. If several rows need to come out, it may be worth cutting and restarting: velvet yarn in a dark colour especially shows pulled-out sections as a duller patch.

items.symptom: Stitch count keeps changing between rows
items.cause: Missing stitches at the edges, or accidentally inserting into the space beside a stitch rather than through the stitch itself.
items.fix: Use stitch markers at both ends on every row and count before working. Hold the fabric stretched slightly across your fingers so the edge stitches open up.

items.symptom: The fabric looks flat and lacks the plush appearance
items.cause: Hook size is too small, compressing the pile. Or the stitches are too tight, squashing the surface fibres.
items.fix: Go up one hook size. Work at a relaxed tension; velvet does not need to be firm to hold its structure.

items.cause: The yarn is shedding cut fibres. This is common in new velvet yarns and usually settles after washing.
items.fix: Shake the piece outdoors before wearing. Wash on a gentle cycle in a mesh bag; the initial wash removes most loose fibres.

content.text: A simple rectangle in double crochet (UK) is the best first velvet project: no shaping, no increases or decreases, just straight rows. Work 20 stitches by 20 rows to get comfortable finding stitches in the pile before attempting a shaped piece like a hat or bag.
